pass_a_gloss:
By considering the union of persons alone as the economy, and gathering the natures into one ineffably and beyond reason, as God himself has known, and not saying a confusion of the natures as if the nature of the Logos were changed into that of man, nor the human into that of the Logos, but thinking of each as existing in its own nature's limit, we say the union has been accomplished by the Logos dwelling bodily in the temple from the virgin, and soon after, if anyone says the union is only of persons, separating the natures completely from each other, he is carried off the straight path, Cyril from the same interpretation, see now also in the two wildernesses the one Christ, that is, God incarnate, and dying bodily for sin, that by the sprinkling of his own blood he might wholly sanctify the Church, and remaining again impassible divinely, Cyril from the interpretation to the Hebrews, if he has perfected us by water and Spirit, how does he not act divinely and humanly at once, the same existing, and how as in one God at once and man? Cyril from the interpretation to the Hebrews, of the second volume, and it happened ineffably and beyond mind that divinity and humanity were united, and though the natures are distinct in confession, yet one and only Son from both.

For if indeed the natures were diverse and unequal to one another among those running together into unity, I mean flesh and God, yet nevertheless one and only Son from both, truly having and to us fittingly to be ensouled by a rational soul the temple united to the Logos, Cyril from the interpretation of the pros Hebraeous epistle, For not was it a man bare and of us one, the according to nature life being able to complete the energy, through this 'by the grace of God' and itself the body of the Logos who became incarnate for us, and yet according to nature being of life, over against the salvation of all he tasted of death, as says himself the most holy Paul, in order that not the work of the earthly body be considered to be to abolish death, but of him indeed rather of the one united to him and existing alongside him according to nature subsisting Logos, 25
pass_b_english: The union of natures is not merely a matter of the union of persons, but rather the natures are gathered into one, ineffably and beyond reason, as God himself has known.

We do not say that there is a confusion or disruption of the natures, as if the nature of the Logos were changed into that of man, or the human into that of the Logos, but rather that each nature remains within its own limit.
The union has been realized by the Logos dwelling bodily in the temple born of the virgin.
If anyone claims that the union is only of persons and completely separates the natures from each other, they stray from the straight path, as Cyril notes in his interpretation.
We see the one Christ, who is God incarnate, dying bodily for sin, so that by the sprinkling of his own blood he may wholly sanctify the Church, and remaining again impassible in his divinity.
As Cyril explains in his interpretation of the pros Hebraeous epistle, if he has perfected us by water and Spirit, then he must act both divinely and humanly at once, being the same one who exists.
It is a mystery that happened ineffably and beyond mind, that divinity and humanity were united, and though the natures are distinct, yet there is one and only Son from both.

Even if the natures were diverse and unequal to one another, and ran together into unity, there is still one and only Son from both, who is truly possessed of a rational soul and is the temple united to the Logos.

As Cyril notes, it was not a bare man, one of us, who could complete the energy of the according-to-nature life, but rather, as the most holy Paul says, it was by the grace of God that the body of the Logos, who became incarnate for us, tasted death, in order that the work of abolishing death might not be attributed to the earthly body, but rather to the Logos who is united to it and subsists alongside it.
The most holy Paul says, 'by the grace of God' (Hebrews 2:9), indicating that it was God's grace that allowed the Logos to taste death for the salvation of all.
